planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Loving Memories rewards a long growing season with repeated flushes of scapes rather than a single bloom period.

directions: Loving Memories produces a heavy flush of pale ivory-white blossoms with a faint chartreuse throat on well-branched, upright scapes that rebloom repeatedly through summer in warm climates. Its exceptional bud count and rebloom habit have made it one of the most widely planted near-white daylilies for mass border plantings and cut-flower use. The semi-evergreen clumps multiply quickly and stay tidy without staking. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to sustain the heaviest bloom flush.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Wilson Spider shows its narrow, twisting petals best where scapes aren't crowded by neighboring perennials.

directions: Wilson Spider is a classic spider-form daylily prized for its long, narrow, twisting gold petals held on tall, airy scapes well above the foliage. Its extreme petal-length-to-width ratio places it firmly among the recognized spider daylilies that helped define the form for collectors in the mid-twentieth century. Clumps are dormant, dying back fully in winter before rebuilding a fresh fan of foliage each spring. Site in full sun with good air movement, since the narrow petals show best where scapes aren't crowded by neighboring perennials.
sources: The Spider and Unusual Form Daylily Society

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Whichford's pale flowers show best against darker-foliaged or darker-flowered companions.

directions: Whichford bears fragrant, creamy ivory-white flowers with a soft lemon throat, among the palest daylily colors available when it was introduced and still valued for that near-white effect in mixed borders. The compact, well-foliaged clumps stay tidy through the season and increase at a moderate, manageable pace. It combines well with darker-toned daylilies and other perennials where its pale flowers read as a highlight rather than being lost. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every four years as clumps become congested.

common_name: Purple d'Oro Daylily (Small Purple Reblooming Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; deadhead spent scapes on Purple d'Oro to encourage continued rebloom through fall.

directions: Bred by Patrick Stamile, Purple d'Oro produces small, gold-throated purple flowers in great abundance on compact, well-branched scapes that keep reblooming from early summer well into fall. Its small flower size and low, grassy foliage make it a popular groundcover-style edging plant, echoing the role Stella de Oro plays among yellow daylilies. Deadheading spent scapes encourages continued rebloom through the season. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every two to three years to keep the clump floriferous.

common_name: Vintage Bordeaux Daylily (Deep Wine-Red Eyed Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile soil in full sun; Vintage Bordeaux's tetraploid substance keeps the wine-red petals from spotting in strong afternoon sun.

directions: Bred by Curt Hanson, Vintage Bordeaux carries rich wine-red petals deepening to a darker maroon eye and picotee edge above a green throat, giving the flower notable depth and contrast. Scapes are well-branched with a high bud count, extending the bloom season on each fan. The tetraploid substance keeps petals from spotting or fading in strong afternoon sun. Plant in full sun in fertile soil and divide every three to four years to maintain strong scape branching.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jason Salter sends up successive scapes rather than a single flush where the growing season is long.

directions: Introduced from Elizabeth Salter's Tuscawilla Gardens breeding program, Jason Salter bears clear rose-pink self-colored flowers with a small green throat on sturdy, well-branched scapes. It reblooms readily in climates with a long growing season, sending up successive scapes rather than a single flush. The semi-evergreen foliage stays attractive through most of the growing year in mild climates. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to keep the clump vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Blueberry Candy's compact size suits rock gardens, containers, and front-of-border plantings.

directions: Part of the small-flowered Candy series, Blueberry Candy carries lavender-blue petals over a chartreuse-green throat, one of the cooler-toned members of a series otherwise known for fruit-colored pastels. Its compact, grassy foliage and small flower size suit rock gardens, containers, and front-of-border plantings where full-sized daylily clumps would overwhelm the space. Established clumps produce a high scape count relative to their size. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every two to three years to prevent overcrowding.

common_name: Wild Horses Daylily (Near-Black Purple Eyed Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Wild Horses' dark petals hold their color best with consistent moisture through bud set.

directions: Wild Horses displays deep purple-black petals surrounding a bold chartreuse-green throat, a high-contrast combination bred to showcase how dark daylily pigmentation can get without the flower reading as flat or muddy. Scapes are well-branched and held above the foliage, keeping the dramatic bicolor effect visible from a distance. The tetraploid substance gives the dark petals enough thickness to resist sun-scorch. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years as the clump thickens.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Tigress's patterned bloom reads best planted where it can be viewed at a moderate distance.

directions: Part of the Tuscawilla series bred at Elizabeth Salter's Florida gardens, Tigress bears bold orange petals overlaid with a darker rust-red pattern radiating from the throat, giving each flower a striking painted appearance. Well-branched scapes hold the patterned blooms above tidy, semi-evergreen foliage. The bold contrast makes it stand out even at a distance in mixed perennial plantings. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to sustain flower size and pattern intensity.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; give Free Wheelin' room so its twisted, quilled petals aren't hidden by neighboring foliage.

directions: Free Wheelin' carries wide, twisted and quilled gold petals that curl and pinch along their length, placing it among the recognized unusual-form daylilies rather than the classic flat-faced types. The twisting, spatulate petals give each bloom a windblown, spinning appearance that stands out in a mixed daylily bed. Scapes are tall and well-branched, holding flowers clear of the foliage mound. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to maintain vigorous scape production.
sources: The Spider and Unusual Form Daylily Society

common_name: Black Ambrosia Daylily (Near-Black Red Self Tetraploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Black Ambrosia's dark pigment develops most fully with consistent moisture during bud formation.

directions: Black Ambrosia produces velvety near-black red flowers with only a small green throat breaking the dark color, making it one of the darkest-flowered daylilies commonly grown in home gardens. Its medium-sized blooms and compact scapes suit smaller borders where a full-sized dark-flowered clump would be too large. The tetraploid substance helps the deep red pigment resist fading in hot afternoon sun. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to maintain flower color and bud count.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Spanish Harlem's saturated color anchors hot-color borders well from midseason on.

directions: Spanish Harlem bears vivid red-orange self-colored flowers with a small yellow-green throat, a saturated warm color that reads strongly even from a distance. Scapes are well-branched and held above a vigorous, fast-multiplying clump. Its intense coloring makes it a popular anchor plant for hot-color borders paired with rudbeckia, crocosmia, and other warm-season perennials. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to keep the clump floriferous.
